sections.title: PTS Lessons
sections.summary: 15 lessons covering every PTS topic, from railway basics to safe positions, lookouts, electrification, emergencies and Sentinel.

blocks.text: The words used in briefings, track layouts and emergency calls. If you know them, you will understand where trains can go and where you can stand.

items: The four-foot is the space between the two rails of one track. The six-foot is between two adjacent tracks. The ten-foot is the wider space between pairs of tracks. The cess is beside the line, beyond the outermost rail.
'On or near the line' means on the line or within 3 metres (10 feet) of it.
Trains can approach on any line, at any time, in either direction. Bi-directional and reversible lines are signalled both ways.
The Up direction is usually towards London or the main centre on a route; check the sectional appendix for local exceptions.
Your location is given by the ELR (Engineer's Line Reference) and mileage. There are 80 chains in a mile; a chain is 22 yards.
Points (switches and crossings) can move at any time without warning. Never put your feet between a switch blade and the stock rail.
Track circuits and axle counters detect trains. Never lay metal across both running rails.
Modern trains can be very quiet, and a train at speed may need well over a kilometre to stop.

blocks.text: Being able to name the lines and give your exact location can save a life in an emergency.
Most of the time you spend near the line is walking to and from work. Use only authorised access points and planned routes.

items: Enter and leave only by authorised access points named in your briefing. Lock gates behind you where required.
You need a reason to be there, the right competence and a safe system of work. Holding PTS alone is not permission.
Walk in the cess or a designated walking route, facing trains on the nearest line where possible. Avoid the four-foot and six-foot.
Cross only when authorised, at right angles, after looking both ways, stepping over rails and equipment rather than on them.
Never cross in front of a stopped train, and never climb under, between or over vehicles.
Carry long items horizontally and low, especially under overhead line equipment.
Check access signs match your briefing. Poor signage has led groups onto the wrong lines (South Hampstead, 2018).
Tell the COSS when you leave the line, and leave before protection is given up.

blocks.text: No safe system of work, no access.
A position of safety keeps you clear of passing trains and the air turbulence they create. You must know where it is before you start work.

items: Line speed up to 100 mph: at least 1.25 m (4 ft) from the nearest rail on which a train may approach.
Line speed over 100 mph and up to 125 mph: at least 2 m (6 ft 6 in) from the nearest rail.
Be in your position of safety at least 10 seconds before the train arrives.
It must be stable, firm and easy to reach, not a sloping edge, troughing lid or narrow ledge.
Face the train, keep clothing fastened, and secure loose items that slipstream could draw in.
Acknowledge a driver's horn by raising one arm above your head once you are clear.
Stay put after a train passes until you are told it is safe. A second train may be hidden by the first.
Limited clearance means there is no position of safety. Do not be there when trains run unless the line is protected.

blocks.text: Distance plus time: the right distance, reached at least 10 seconds early.
Warning systems tell you a train is coming so you can get clear. They do not stop trains. Lookout working is now the last resort on Network Rail.

items: Minimum warning time = time to stop work, clear equipment and walk to safety, plus 10 seconds.
Sighting distance needed = train speed × warning time. 1 mph ≈ 0.447 m/s, so 100 mph ≈ 44.7 m/s.
Example: 100 mph with 25 s warning needs about 1,118 m of sighting.
ATWS detects trains automatically. TOWS is fixed lineside equipment triggered by trains. LOWS uses a lookout to trigger site warnings.
A lookout must be competent, fit, briefed, in a position of safety, and do no other work. No phones and no radios for train warnings.
If sighting reduces (fog, darkness, glare, curves), the lookout warns the group to stop and tells the COSS.
From December 2025, Network Rail restricted lookout working to situations where no safer option exists. Relay (distant and intermediate) lookouts are banned.
Respond to every warning at once. Never ignore a warning you think is a false alarm.

blocks.text: Warnings rely on people reacting in time; protection does not.

topics.title: Safe systems of work
topics.reference: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles

blocks.text: A safe system of work is the planned way a group is protected from trains. Planners use the hierarchy and pick the safest practicable option.

items: Hierarchy, safest first: safeguarded (lines blocked), fenced, separated (2 m gap with a site warden), automatic warning, lookout warning.
A line blockage means the signaller keeps protecting signals at danger and lets no trains in. A possession is a longer closure for engineering work.
The PICOP manages the possession; the Engineering Supervisor (ES) manages each worksite; the COSS (or person in charge) protects the group.
Engineering trains and on-track plant can still move inside a possession.
The COSS must brief you on site, check competences and stay with the group. Do not sign a briefing you do not understand.
If the planned protection is refused or unavailable, the work must not go ahead using a less safe improvised method (lesson from Margam, 2019).
Anyone can stop unsafe work. Network Rail's Worksafe procedure protects your right to refuse.
Report hazards and near misses through Close Call, or confidentially through CIRAS.

blocks.text: Separating people from trains is the most effective control.
Most GB mainline electrification is 25,000 volts AC. It can arc across a gap, so distance is your protection.

items: Treat OLE as live at all times unless you are told it is isolated and earthed.
Keep yourself and anything you carry at least 2.75 m (9 ft) from live OLE.
Never climb on vehicles, wagons, masts or structures under OLE unless authorised.
Carry long items horizontally and low. Never use water jets, kites, drones or ropes near the wires.
Fallen or damaged wires may be live, and so may anything they touch, including rails, fences and the ground.
Isolations are arranged by authorised people under permit arrangements; earths protect against re-energising and induced voltage.
If someone is in contact with OLE, do not touch them. Get the power switched off through the signaller or electrical control.
Report OLE damage with the exact location.

blocks.text: Keep away, keep low, treat as live.
Much of southern England uses a conductor rail at up to 750 V DC. It is at ground level, where feet and tools can easily touch it.

items: Treat the conductor rail as live at all times unless an isolation has been confirmed.
Never touch or step on the conductor rail or its guard boards. Never step between the conductor rail and the running rail.
Gaps and ramp ends do not make the rail safe; trains' shoe gear can bridge gaps and is live.
Keep metal tools, tape measures, ladders and liquids away from the conductor rail; bridging it to a running rail causes a violent flash.
Take extra care in darkness, snow and flooding, which hide or energise the rail.
Isolations use conductor rail permits; short-circuiting devices protect isolated rail.
Do not touch a casualty near the conductor rail until isolation is confirmed.
Your PTS must include the DCCR module to work on DC lines.

blocks.text: Never touch it, never step on it, always treat it as live.
In an emergency, stop trains first through the signaller, keep yourself safe, then get help.

items: Report obstructions, broken rails, landslips and fires to the signaller at once, using a signal post telephone if nearby.
Give your name, role, exact location (ELR, mileage, line name, signal number) and what has happened. Repeat key details back.
Call 999 (or 112) for emergency services, and tell the signaller so the railway can respond.
To stop a train in an emergency: show a red flag or red light, or any light waved violently, or raise both arms above your head, from a position of safety.
Emergency protection with detonators is only done by trained people: three detonators 20 m apart, normally about 2 km from the obstruction, plus track circuit operating clips.
Never put yourself in danger to help. Check for electrical hazards before touching a casualty.
Report every accident and near miss. RAIB investigates to learn lessons, not to blame.

blocks.text: Stop the trains, stay safe, raise the alarm.
PPE is the last line of defence. It helps you be seen and protects against some hazards, but it cannot protect you from a train.

items: Railway high-visibility clothing is orange to RIS-3279-TOM (previously GO/RT3279). Yellow is not used on track.
Keep hi-vis clean, fastened and uncovered. Network Rail requires orange clothing that covers arms and legs for most work.
Safety boots need toe protection and ankle support. Wear helmets, eye protection, gloves and hearing protection as the task requires.
Hearing protection must never stop you hearing warnings; noisy work needs suitable warning arrangements.
No personal headphones on or near the line.
Your sponsor provides PPE; you must wear it and look after it. Replace damaged or faded items.
Check tools before use, keep guards fitted, and account for every tool at the end of work.

blocks.text: Being seen does not mean the train can stop.
Track work is safety-critical. Alcohol, drugs, some medicines, fatigue and illness all reduce your ability to react.

items: Network Rail's alcohol limit is 29 mg per 100 ml of blood (13 µg per 100 ml of breath), far lower than the 80 mg drink-drive limit in England and Wales.
Testing includes pre-appointment, random, for-cause and post-incident. Refusing a test is treated as a positive result.
Under Network Rail's updated policy, a positive test can mean losing PTS and your Sentinel card for five years.
Only time removes alcohol. Coffee, food and sleep do not speed it up.
Declare medicines that may cause drowsiness and get advice before working.
Sentinel rules: do not report for duty within 12 hours of a previous shift on the infrastructure unless risk-assessed and controlled.
Network Rail's fatigue standard uses trigger conditions; for example, over 60 hours in 7 rolling days needs a fatigue plan, and controls include no lookout duties.
If you are too tired or unwell to work safely, say so and stay off the line.

blocks.text: Fit for duty means fit on the day, not just on paper.
Sentinel records the identity and competences of people working on Network Rail managed infrastructure.

items: Carry your Sentinel card whenever you are on Network Rail managed infrastructure, and show it when asked.
Never lend your card or use anyone else's. Report a lost or damaged card to your sponsor straight away.
Your Primary Sponsor is responsible for you, including your competence, medical, drugs and alcohol status, PPE and working hours.
PTS is valid for two years. Recertify within 56 days of expiry or you must take the initial course again.
Only carry out roles you hold valid competence for. A suspended or expired competence must not be used.
Report anything that affects your ability to work safely, including medication and personal circumstances.
Track visitors without PTS must be escorted under an approved visitor arrangement.

blocks.text: Your card proves who you are and what you are competent to do.
Clear, confirmed communication stops misunderstandings that put people in front of trains.

items: Start every safety-critical call with your name, role and exact location.
Repeat back key details and close the loop. Do not just say 'OK'.
Use the phonetic alphabet for letters (Alpha, Bravo, Charlie...) and say numbers digit by digit when they could be confused.
Use proper line names such as 'Up Fast', not 'left' or 'right'.
Signals control trains, not your protection. Red = stop; single yellow = be prepared to stop at the next signal; double yellow = preliminary caution; green = proceed.
Hand-held radios and phones must not be used to give train warnings.
Raise one arm above your head to acknowledge a driver's horn.

blocks.text: If you did not hear it clearly, you did not hear it.
Real sites throw up situations the briefing did not mention. Stop, think and get clear first.

items: If you see or hear a train, get clear. Do not wait for a warning.
Never cross in front of an approaching train to reach a position of safety; use one on your side.
Watch for things that reduce sighting or hearing: curves, cuttings, fog, glare, wind, darkness, noise and PPE.
Junctions, crossovers and diversions mean trains can appear on unexpected lines.
Plant and engineering trains can move inside possessions and have blind spots.
If site conditions differ from the plan, stop and tell the COSS before carrying on.
Challenge informal shortcuts such as 'we always do it this way'. They have killed people.

blocks.text: If in doubt, get out.
The Rail Accident Investigation Branch (RAIB) investigates to find causes and prevent repeats. Its findings explain why the rules exist.

items: Since 2005, RAIB has investigated about 67 events involving track workers and moving trains; 10 caused deaths.
By the end of 2023, over 99% of Network Rail work activities were done on lines closed to traffic.
Unassisted lookout working had fallen to about 1% of activities in 2023, and was linked to many accidents.
Common causes: informal unsafe practices, weak supervision, poor information and signage, time pressure and reluctance to challenge.
Managers need to see what happens on site, not just check paperwork.

blocks.text: Every rule in your PTS course was learned the hard way.
Network Rail's ten Lifesaving Rules target the activities that cause most deaths and life-changing injuries.

items: Risk areas include contact with trains, working with electricity, working at height, moving equipment, driving and personal responsibility.
Electricity: never assume equipment is isolated; it must be proven dead before you touch it.
Driving: always wear a seat belt, never speed, never use a phone (even hands-free), never drive under the influence.
Work at height needs planned fall protection. Stay out of exclusion zones around plant and never stand under a raised load.
Fair Culture aims to understand why rules were broken and respond fairly, so people report honestly.
Use the hierarchy of control: eliminate, engineer, administer, then PPE.
Intervene when you see unsafe behaviour; anyone can stop the job.

blocks.text: Home safe every day.

sections.title: Key Numbers & Glossary
sections.summary: The distances, speeds and terms you must know.

rows: Position of safety up to 100 mph
About 4 ft from the nearest rail on which a train may approach.
About 6 ft 6 in, for line speeds above 100 mph and up to 125 mph.
Be in your position of safety at least 10 seconds before the train arrives.
On the line, or within 3 m (10 ft) of it.
Minimum gap from the open line, controlled by a site warden.
Keep yourself and anything you carry at least 2.75 m (9 ft) from live OLE.
Third-rail lines, mainly in southern England.
Per 100 ml of blood (13 µg per 100 ml of breath). Drink-drive limit in England and Wales: 80 mg.
Sentinel rules: no duty within 12 hours of a previous shift on the infrastructure unless risk-assessed.
More than 60 hours in 7 rolling days needs a fatigue assessment and plan.
Recertify within 56 days of expiry, or retake the initial course.
Trained staff place three detonators 20 m apart, normally about 2 km from the obstruction.
Multiply mph by 0.447. 60 mph covers about one mile per minute.
30 questions, 40 minutes, pass mark 24 (80%). A practice format, not the official assessment.
An authorised place to enter or leave the railway.
Automatic Track Warning System. Detects trains and gives warnings at the site.
Automatic Warning System. Gives the driver an in-cab warning about the signal ahead.
Train detection that counts axles into and out of a section.
Stones that hold sleepers in place and drain the track.
A line signalled for trains in either direction.
The area beside the track beyond the outermost rail.
A confidential reporting service for safety concerns.
Network Rail's system for reporting hazards and near misses.
The extra rail that supplies DC power to trains (third rail).
Controller of Site Safety. Sets up and manages the safe system of work for a group.
Where the line runs below the surrounding ground.
DC conductor rail. The PTS module for third-rail lines.
A device clipped to the rail that bangs when a train runs over it, warning the driver.
Engineer's Line Reference. A code that, with the mileage, identifies a location.
A raised bank of earth carrying the railway.
Manages a worksite within a possession.
A barrier physically stops people reaching the open line.
Close enough that a train could strike you or your equipment.
The space between the two rails of one track.
The railway's radio system for drivers and signallers.
Individual Working Alone. A separate competence for low-risk work by one person.
A place with no position of safety when a train passes.
A line closed to trains, with protecting signals held at danger.
Lookout Operated Warning System. A lookout triggers warnings given by equipment at the site.
A competent person who watches for trains and warns the group in time.
Overhead line equipment, usually 25 kV AC.
Machines that work on the track, such as road-rail vehicles.
Person in Charge of the Possession.
Switches and crossings that let trains change tracks. They can move without warning.
A place far enough from the line to be safe when a train passes.
A line closed to normal traffic for engineering work.
The organisation responsible for you under Sentinel.
Personal Track Safety. The basic competence for working on or near the line.
Rail Accident Investigation Branch. Investigates accidents to improve safety.
Working on or near a line open to trains, relying on warnings.
A recess in a tunnel, bridge or wall where you can stand clear of trains.
A line used for normal train movements.
The planned arrangements that protect people from trains.
The planned documents for a job and its safe system of work.
The scheme recording identity and competences of NRMI workers.
A 2 m gap is kept from the open line, controlled by a site warden.
A line for stabling or loading, not through running.
Warns anyone about to leave the safe area towards an open line.
The space between two adjacent tracks.
Signal post telephone. Connects directly to the signaller.
Track circuit operating clip. Makes a line show as occupied.
The wider space between two pairs of running lines.
Train Operated Warning System. Fixed equipment triggered by approaching trains.
Train Protection and Warning System. Can apply a train's brakes automatically.
Network Rail procedure protecting your right to refuse unsafe work.
A defined area of work inside a possession.

sections.title: RAIB Case Studies
sections.summary: Lessons from real railway accidents investigated by the Rail Accident Investigation Branch (RAIB).

blocks.text: Two track workers were struck and killed by a train while working on a line open to traffic without formally appointed lookouts. A third narrowly escaped.
Never fall back on informal or less safe methods. Planning must not allow a downgrade when a line blockage is refused, and managers must see what happens on site.
A track worker was struck during a track inspection that relied on unassisted lookout working.
Lookout warning is the least safe system. The accident sped up Network Rail's move away from lookout working.
A worker was struck shortly after placing possession protection, having moved outside the protected area. The labour supplier had not checked the worker's hours.
Placing or removing protection is high risk. Stay within protected limits, and manage hours for everyone, including contingent workers.

Six workers nearly collided with a 75 mph train on a bridge with no position of safety. The COSS had used an unauthorised system with radio warnings; a warning was not received. Three jumped onto the parapet.
Never use radios for train warnings or improvise a safe system of work. Challenge plans that do not suit the site.
A lookout moved into the path of a train and was killed. The COSS had not monitored the team.
Lookouts are at risk too and must stay in a position of safety. Leaders must supervise actively.
A welder was struck by a train. Peer pressure, leadership failings and reluctance to interrupt work were factors.
Never let time pressure or the wish to finish stop you getting clear or speaking up.
A structures examination team crossed a viaduct at track level and narrowly avoided a 125 mph train.
Structures with limited clearance must be planned so nobody is on them when trains can run.
Workers went onto the wrong lines, partly because track layout signage was missing, and had about two seconds' warning.
Check access signs and line names against your briefing every time.
A group had to jump clear of a train with under two seconds' warning after confusion about the lookout's role. Contract staff felt unable to challenge.
Everyone, whatever their contract, must feel able to challenge unsafe work.
A COSS unknowingly used a safe work pack for a different location and had not fully read the documents for a familiar task.
Familiar jobs still need the plan checked against the actual site.
Four track workers clearing snow were killed. There was no clearly defined leader or lookout arrangement.
This led to the role that became today's COSS: one clear person in charge of the group's safety.
